## Summary

`list_tickets` against this store can terminate with `MCP request failed: Transport closed` and
no structured error payload — the caller cannot tell whether the query was invalid, the server
failed, or the response was simply too large.

## PROVEN root cause (Phase 1, 2026-08-28)

Unfiltered `tools/call list_tickets {}` against `https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/mcp`
(Streamable HTTP, bearer auth) returned `http=200`, **94,541,551 bytes over 177.29 seconds**, in
one well-formed SSE `event: message` frame. **The server does not fail.** The CLIENT abandons a
94.5 MB / 177 s single response, and how it abandons is client-specific: Copilot CLI reports
`Transport closed`; a Claude Code session with a 30 s connect budget times out; a third client
succeeded but spilled 219,815 chars to disk. None can distinguish "too big" from "server died",
because the server offers no bound and no structured signal.

## Reconciliation with `unreal-milky-sloth` (`6fe7-956f-4901-45cf`) — read this before fixing

That sibling **REFUTED the response-size hypothesis, and was right to on its evidence**: its
failing call was 50,532 bytes while another client succeeded at ~219,000 ("size does not
discriminate"); its symptom was `TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt`, a type error,
not a size or timeout error; and post-fix it live-validated `ready_tickets` returning 939,719
characters successfully.

Both findings stand, because they are about **different failures**:

* `unreal-milky-sloth`: the server emitted bare 19-digit integers and a JS client threw while
  parsing. Fixed and live-validated; `js_safe_result` now quotes them.
* **this ticket**: measured **after** that fix shipped, the payload parses cleanly — and is
  94.5 MB. That is not a serialization defect; it is an unbounded payload.

Therefore the **219,815-character datum is NOT evidence for this ticket's cause and is not used
as such.** At 4.3x the size of a failing call it discriminates nothing, exactly as the sibling
argued. The discriminating evidence is the 94.5 MB / 177 s measurement taken post-fix, which
BigInt cannot explain. The other two original candidates are closed: BigInt **REJECTED** (the
call completes and parses); deploy cutover **REJECTED** (reproducible on demand three days after
the 18:54:29Z container replacement, from a session that was never orphaned).

## The guard that already exists, and why it is not enough

This is **not greenfield**. `list_tickets` is already lean-by-default (`full: bool = False`),
dropping `description` and `comments`. Measured on this store (2,855 tickets) that saves 39%
(73.0 MB full -> 44.4 MB lean) and leaves the bulk untouched: of the **lean** payload,
`authorship_ledger` is 59%, `attestations` 23%, `signature` 6% — **88% is base64 DSSE signature
material** no list caller consumes. Per row: 15,548 bytes lean vs 1,726 with those four (plus
`keyring`) dropped. `ready_tickets` has **no lean mode and no limit at all** (61 rows, 693,556
bytes). The one payload bound that does exist — `_cap_workflow_payload`, 90,000 bytes, whose
comment states "under the client's ~25K-token budget" — is wired only to `get_workflow_status`
and `get_workflow_result`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] The cause is identified and explicitly reconciled with both sibling tickets (above).

- [ ] **One shared lean projection.** A single function — `lean_projection` over a
      `LEAN_OMITTED_FIELDS` tuple in `src/rebar/_engine_support/reads.py` — is the only spelling
      of the lean row, and drops `authorship_ledger`, `attestations`, `signature` and `keyring`
      in addition to `description` and `comments`. It is called by BOTH read backends: the
      event-log path (`list_states`) and the snapshot path
      (`_snapshot/ticket_view.py::TicketView.list_by_query`). `ready_tickets` cannot reach it
      through the library — `rebar.ready` -> `ready_states` -> `public_state` has no
      `include_body`/`full` plumbing — and this plan deliberately does NOT add that plumbing to
      `ready_states`; instead the MCP tool applies the same `lean_projection` at the tool layer
      (`_mcp_reads._discovery_rows`), so both discovery surfaces and both backends share one
      function. `full=True` restores the previous bytes exactly.

- [ ] **Bounded, and measured at a named seam.** `list_tickets` AND `ready_tickets` are bounded
      at the same **90,000-byte** `_WORKFLOW_TOKEN_BUDGET_BYTES` the workflow cap already
      enforces. Measuring the raw reducer rows under-estimates the real payload, so the
      measurement is taken on the validated rows. The seam: the bound runs INSIDE the tool body,
      after `TicketStateOut.model_validate`, and CALLS `js_safe_result` on those rows itself
      rather than waiting for the error-guard wrapper, which applies that transform only after
      the body has returned. Applying the same pure function to the same rows makes the measured
      bytes equal the bytes the guard will emit, while keeping the raise point inside the body
      where a structured error is still deliverable.

- [ ] **Structured refusal, in the closed vocabulary, with the right exception TYPE.**
      Exceeding the budget raises a **`rebar._errors.RebarError`** — the type matters, not just
      the attribute: `install_error_guard`'s `_envelope_error` only enveloped a known rebar
      exception type, so a plain `Exception` carrying an `.error_code` attribute would be
      dropped and the caller would get an unstructured failure. It carries
      `error_code="response_too_large"` and is delivered through the existing envelope seam,
      naming the match count, the byte size, the budget, and a remedy. Never a partial list (a
      short list cannot be told from a complete one); never a bare transport close. The new
      value is added to the closed `rebar.KNOWN_ERROR_CODES` vocabulary in
      `src/rebar/_errors.py` and to `tests/unit/api_surface_baseline.json`. `error_code_for`
      needs no change (precedence step 5 already returns a non-empty `exc.error_code`), and no
      schema change is needed (`common.schema.json#/$defs/error_envelope.error` is an open
      string, not an enum).

- [ ] **The remedy named in the refusal must be one the REFUSED TOOL can execute.** A remedy
      the tool would reject is a dead end, and the two list surfaces differ: `list_tickets`
      accepts `status`/`ticket_type`/`priority`/`parent`/`has_tag`/`without_tag`, while
      **`ready_tickets` accepts only `sort` and `full` — it has no filter arguments at all**, so
      a shared "narrow the query with has_tag" message would name parameters it rejects.
      `ready_tickets`' refusal must instead point at `next_batch(epic_id)`, the scoped
      conflict-aware view of the same unblocked work.

- [ ] **State the headroom, because it is thin and it decides when this bites.** Measured on
      this store: `ready_tickets` is 59 rows / **88,480 wire bytes against the 90,000-byte
      budget — 1.7% of headroom, ~1,499 bytes per row**, so roughly ONE more ready ticket makes
      the default call refuse. That is accepted deliberately rather than papered over by
      inflating the budget (the budget is the client's real constraint; raising it moves the
      failure back into the client where it has no structured signal). It is the reason the
      previous criterion is not cosmetic: `ready_tickets` refusing is a foreseeable near-term
      state, so its refusal has to hand the caller a working next step. Recorded in
      `docs/release-notes.md` alongside the narrowing.

- [ ] **Any surface whose DEFAULT output narrows** as a result is recorded as a pre-1.0 breaking
      change in `docs/release-notes.md` and `CHANGELOG.md`, with the measured before/after and
      the opt-out flag.

- [ ] **Regression coverage asserts the error's CONTENTS, not merely that a refusal happened.**
      A synthetic store of >=4,000 rows is refused AND the envelope is checked for
      `error_code == "response_too_large"`, the match count, the byte size, the budget value and
      the narrowing-filter names. An under-budget list is returned whole and unmodified. One case
      covers the regression window specifically: rows whose RAW-dict size is under budget while
      the wire payload is over it must still be refused.

- [ ] **LIVE VALIDATION — REQUIRED TO CLOSE.** `list_tickets` and `ready_tickets` called through
      the deployed endpoint return results (or a structured limit error) with no transport close.
      **Auth precondition:** `https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/mcp` is behind the OAuth gate,
      so the validating client MUST present a valid OAuth bearer token; a `401`/`403` is a FAILED
      validation, not an environment excuse. Evidence must be OBSERVED against that deployed
      server and recorded in a ticket comment naming the tool(s) called, the arguments, and the
      actual response. A passing local test does NOT satisfy this criterion, and neither does a
      merged change: the container must have redeployed and served the call. This exists because
      a fix here was previously reported complete on the strength of a merge while the deployed
      behaviour was still broken.
